question: The European music industry is witnessing moves by music streaming services to reform their royalty allocation models. Many in the sector agree that reform is needed to address fraud and dilution, and to make streaming fairer and more diverse.

However, certain aspects of the different reforms are raising concern, as it appears that revenue is being shifted towards the bigger companies – in an extremely concentrated market – and potentially resulting in discrimination against and market exclusion of smaller artists and competitors.

The European Parliament recently approved a report calling on the Commission to assess the allocation of revenue from streaming services and the impact of concentration on the music market, in view of a fairer and more culturally diverse European music streaming market. In the light of the above: 1.

Will the Commission gather information from the services and major music companies concerned to understand the origins of the reforms, who was involved in the negotiations and how the final terms were agreed upon, in order to prepare an assessment on the impact these changes will have on competition and cultural diversity, and can it share who will be consulted on any revisions?
Would an EU music observatory aid in understanding and monitoring the market, thus facilitating collective solutions?
answer: The Commission is aware of the market dynamics related to the European music industry and acknowledges that more comprehensive and transparent data would be useful to better understand the market, as also confirmed in a feasibility study for a European music observatory, published in 2020 (1).

In 2022, the Commission published a report on ‘Measuring the Cultural and Creative Sectors in the EU’ (2), which included testing a methodology to measure music digital services. As a follow-up, a Task Force has been set up within Eurostat to work on defining new EU cultural statistics to be implemented from 2025.

Its work specifically includes the enhancement of statistical measurement of cultural sub-sectors, including the music sector. The need for more music-related data is also why several ongoing Music Moves Europe research projects under Horizon Europe are investigating this.

In addition, in April 2024, the Commission launched a study to gather information on the discoverability of diverse European cultural content online, including the music sector (3). Results are expected in the second half of 2025.

According to the competition rules of the EU, agreements between undertakings, decisions by associations of undertakings and concerted practices which may affect trade between Member States and which have as their object or effect the prevention, restriction or distortion of competition within the internal market are prohibited (Article 101 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union — ‘TFEU’).

Moreover, it is also prohibited for an undertaking to abuse its dominant position within the internal market or in a substantial part of it, insofar as it may affect trade between Member States (Article 102 of the TFEU). The Commission is monitoring the music streaming markets and will use its powers, including its competences to enforce the above provisions, if necessary for ensuring a level playing field.

The Commission is also monitoring the implementation of Chapter III of Directive 2019/790/EU (4) which introduced provisions related to the fair remuneration in exploitation contracts of authors and performers.
